questions.q: Cotton leaf curl virus is carried from one cotton plant to another mainly by:
questions.x: Cotton leaf curl virus is transmitted by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) as it feeds on the phloem sap; controlling whiteflies reduces the disease.

questions.q: The capsid of a virus together with the nucleic acid enclosed in it is called the:
questions.x: Capsid plus genome is the nucleocapsid. A capsomere is a single protein subunit of the capsid, and the envelope is the outer lipid layer of some viruses.

questions.q: A nurse is accidentally pricked by a needle just used on an HIV-positive patient. This is an example of HIV exposure through:
questions.x: A needle-stick injury carries a small amount of infected blood directly into the body. HIV is not spread by air, food or saliva on intact skin.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an intermediate of the Krebs cycle?
questions.x: Pyruvate is made in glycolysis and is converted into acetyl CoA before anything enters the cycle. Citrate, oxaloacetate and malate are all compounds of the Krebs cycle itself.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of one mole of ATP to ADP and phosphate releases about:
questions.x: Removing the terminal phosphate of ATP releases about 7.3 kcal (roughly 31 kJ) per mole. About 686 kcal is the energy of complete oxidation of one mole of glucose.

questions.q: Which of the following reactions is catabolic?
o: Formation of a protein from amino acids
questions.x: Catabolic reactions break large molecules into smaller ones, as when glycogen is hydrolysed to glucose. The other three build macromolecules by condensation, which is anabolism.

questions.q: In a plasma lipoprotein particle, triglycerides and cholesterol esters are found:
o: On the outer surface, in contact with the plasma
Inside the chain of amino acids of the protein
Dissolved freely in the plasma around the particle
In the core, surrounded by a shell of phospholipids and proteins
questions.x: The water-insoluble lipids sit in the centre of the particle. Phospholipids and proteins form the outer shell, with their polar parts facing the watery plasma.

questions.q: The prefix 'glyco-' in glycoprotein and glycolipid shows that these molecules contain:
questions.x: 'Glyco-' refers to sugar: glycoproteins and glycolipids carry carbohydrate chains. Glycerol is an alcohol and is not what the prefix means.

questions.q: Although it carries the code for every protein, the type of RNA that makes up the smallest share of a cell's total RNA is:
o: None, as all three are present in equal amounts
questions.x: rRNA is by far the most abundant RNA and tRNA comes next; mRNA forms only a small fraction of the total, partly because it is short-lived.

questions.q: The correct order of the levels of protein structure, from simplest to most complex, is:
questions.x: The amino acid sequence (primary) coils into helices and sheets (secondary), which fold into a 3-D shape (tertiary); several chains may then combine (quaternary).

questions.q: Which type of RNA varies most in length from one molecule to another?
o: tRNA, because each kind carries a different amino acid
mRNA, because its length depends on the gene it is copied from
rRNA, because every ribosome is a different size
None, because all RNA molecules have the same length
questions.x: Each mRNA is a copy of a particular gene, and genes code for polypeptides of very different lengths. tRNA molecules are all small and similar in size.

questions.q: In a typical cell, which nucleic acid makes up the larger share of the cell's mass?
o: DNA, because every cell has a full set of genes
Both are always present in exactly equal amounts
Neither, because nucleic acids are absent from the cytoplasm
questions.x: Cells contain many ribosomes, so RNA (about 6% of a bacterial cell) far exceeds DNA (about 1%). Each cell has only one copy or a few copies of its DNA, and RNA is abundant in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: During digestion, starch is broken down into maltose by the enzyme:
questions.x: Amylase (in saliva and pancreatic juice) hydrolyses starch to maltose. Maltase then breaks maltose to glucose; lipase acts on fats and pepsin on proteins.

questions.q: In sickle-cell haemoglobin, which change is found in each beta chain?
o: Valine at position 6 is replaced by glutamic acid
Glutamic acid at position 6 is replaced by valine
Lysine at position 6 is replaced by glycine
A disulphide bond between two chains is lost
questions.x: Sickle-cell haemoglobin has valine instead of glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta chain. This single change alters the shape of the molecule and of the red cell.

questions.q: The 3′ end of a DNA strand carries a free:
o: Hydroxyl group on carbon 3 of deoxyribose
Phosphate group on carbon 5 of deoxyribose
Hydroxyl group on carbon 2 of deoxyribose
questions.x: At the 3′ end, the last deoxyribose has a free –OH on its carbon 3. The 5′ end has a free phosphate on carbon 5. Deoxyribose has no –OH on carbon 2.

questions.q: Compared with a carbohydrate molecule of similar size, a fat molecule contains:
o: Far fewer oxygen atoms in proportion to its carbon and hydrogen
Far more oxygen atoms in proportion to its carbon and hydrogen
questions.x: Fats are made mostly of C–H chains and contain little oxygen, which is why they release more energy on oxidation. Ordinary fats contain no nitrogen or phosphorus.

questions.q: In a chloroplast, chlorophyll is located in the:
questions.x: Chlorophyll and other pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes, which are stacked into grana. The stroma is the fluid around them.

questions.q: Cells lining the small intestine have many tiny finger-like extensions of the plasma membrane called microvilli. Their main role is to:
o: Increase the surface area for absorption
Move food along the gut by beating
questions.x: Microvilli greatly increase the absorbing surface. They do not beat; movement of material by beating is done by cilia.

questions.q: Cyanobacteria resemble green plants because they:
o: Have chloroplasts surrounded by double membranes
Have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope
Contain chlorophyll a and give off oxygen in photosynthesis
Have cell walls made of cellulose
questions.x: Cyanobacteria are prokaryotes without chloroplasts, but they have chlorophyll a on internal membranes and release oxygen as plants do. Their walls contain peptidoglycan.

questions.q: Specialised plastids that store oils are elaioplasts, while those that store proteins are:
questions.x: Aleuroplasts store protein and elaioplasts store oils; amyloplasts store starch. All three are types of colourless leucoplast.

questions.q: Ribosomes in a eukaryotic cell occur both free in the cytoplasm and attached to the ER, but in a prokaryotic cell they:
o: Are attached only to the nuclear envelope
Lie only free in the cytoplasm, because there is no ER
Are attached only to the cell wall
questions.x: Prokaryotes have no endoplasmic reticulum, so all their ribosomes are free in the cytoplasm.

questions.q: When the effector of a reflex arc is a gland, the response it produces is:
questions.x: Glands respond by secreting, for example saliva or tears. Contraction is the response of a muscle effector, and detecting a stimulus is the job of the receptor.

questions.q: Nodes of Ranvier are present only in:
o: The cell body of a neuron
questions.x: Nodes of Ranvier are the gaps between segments of the myelin sheath, so they exist only where there is myelin.

questions.q: In biology, a stimulus is best defined as:
o: A nerve impulse travelling from the brain to a muscle
A chemical released at the end of an axon
A change in the internal or external environment that can be detected by a receptor
The response made by a muscle or gland
questions.x: A stimulus is any detectable change inside or outside the body. The response is made by an effector, and a chemical released at an axon ending is a neurotransmitter.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a chemoreceptor?
questions.x: A Pacinian corpuscle responds to pressure, so it is a mechanoreceptor. Smell, taste and carotid body cells all respond to chemicals.

questions.q: Besides being faster, saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres saves energy because:
o: Myelinated neurons never need any ATP
Ions cross the membrane only at the nodes, so the pump has less to restore
Myelinated fibres have no sodium–potassium pumps
questions.x: With ion flow limited to the nodes, fewer Na+ and K+ ions move per impulse, so less ATP is spent by the pump restoring the gradients. Pumps and ATP are still needed.

questions.q: A child who has had several painful injections starts crying as soon as she sees a syringe. This response is:
questions.x: The sight of a syringe causes crying only because it has become linked with pain through past experience, so the response is learned: a conditioned reflex. A newborn would not respond this way.

questions.q: A puffer-fish toxin blocks the voltage-gated Na+ channels of axons. The direct effect on these axons is that they:
questions.x: Depolarisation needs the inflow of Na+ through voltage-gated channels. With them blocked, threshold cannot lead to an action potential, so conduction stops.

questions.q: The pons gets its name, meaning 'bridge', because it:
o: Joins the left and right cerebral hemispheres
Contains fibres linking the medulla, cerebellum and higher parts of the brain
Joins the brain to the skull
Joins the pituitary gland to the hypothalamus
questions.x: The pons is a bulge of the brainstem full of nerve fibres that bridge the medulla, the cerebellum and the parts above. The cerebral hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum, not the pons.

questions.q: When an end product switches off its own pathway, the type of control involved is:
questions.x: A rise in the end product switches off its own production, and a fall allows production to resume: a negative feedback loop.

questions.q: The large part of an enzyme molecule outside its active site mainly:
o: Holds the active site in its correct three-dimensional shape
questions.x: Only a few amino acids form the active site; the rest of the folded protein keeps the active site in the precise shape needed for binding and catalysis.

questions.q: The breakdown of hydrogen peroxide can occur with no catalyst, with colloidal platinum, or with catalase. Which ranking of the activation energy, from highest to lowest, is correct?
o: No catalyst, then platinum, then catalase
Catalase, then platinum, then no catalyst
Platinum, then no catalyst, then catalase
Platinum, then catalase, then no catalyst
questions.x: Any catalyst lowers the activation energy, but enzymes lower it far more than inorganic catalysts. So the uncatalysed reaction has the highest barrier and the catalase reaction the lowest.

questions.q: In some enzyme experiments, tubes are placed in ice at a chosen time. This is done to:
o: Stop the reaction at that time without destroying the enzyme
questions.x: At very low temperature enzyme activity almost stops, but the enzyme is not denatured. This 'freezes' the reaction at a known moment.

questions.q: Why did finches on different Galápagos islands become different species?
o: Their populations were isolated on separate islands and each was selected for the local foods
All the finches changed their beaks by using them in different ways
The birds on all islands interbred freely and mixed their traits
A single mutation produced all the species at the same time
questions.x: Isolation stopped interbreeding between island populations, and natural selection on each island favoured beaks suited to the available food. Over time the populations became separate species.

questions.q: The rise in frequency of dark-coloured peppered moths in industrial areas of England is called:
questions.x: Industrial melanism is the increase of dark (melanic) forms in areas darkened by industrial soot, caused by bird predation favouring the dark moths.

questions.q: Lamarck's first law is the law of use and disuse. His second law states that:
o: The fittest individuals survive and reproduce
Changes gained by an individual during life are passed to its offspring
questions.x: Lamarck's second law is the inheritance of acquired characters: changes produced by use or disuse are handed to the next generation.

questions.q: Cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli have all been produced from a single wild mustard species. This is an example of:
questions.x: Farmers chose and bred plants with enlarged leaves, flower buds or stems over many generations, producing these vegetables. This is artificial selection.

questions.q: If 25 primary spermatocytes and 25 primary oocytes all complete meiosis, how many functional gametes are formed?
questions.x: Each primary spermatocyte gives four sperm (25 × 4 = 100). Each primary oocyte gives only one functional ovum, the other products being polar bodies.

questions.q: Which pairing of a sexually transmitted disease with the type of its causative agent is correct?
questions.x: Genital herpes and AIDS are caused by viruses (HSV and HIV). Gonorrhoea and syphilis are caused by bacteria.

questions.q: Both ovaries of a 30-year-old woman are surgically removed. Which change is expected?
o: Her cycles continue, with normal FSH and LH
Her cycles stop, and FSH and LH levels rise
Her cycles stop, and FSH and LH levels fall
Her progesterone rises, and FSH and LH fall
questions.x: Without ovaries, no oestrogen or progesterone is made, so the endometrium is no longer built up. With no negative feedback, the pituitary releases more FSH and LH.

questions.q: In a person with gout, uric acid may also form deposits outside the joints, for example as:
questions.x: Uric acid is excreted by the kidneys, and at high levels it can crystallise there to form kidney stones. Arterial plaques and gallstones have other causes.

questions.q: The entire skeleton of a shark is made of:
questions.x: Sharks belong to the cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes), whose skeleton is made entirely of cartilage. Chitin forms the exoskeleton of arthropods, not of fish.

questions.q: Which type of muscle has the longest cells, some running for several centimetres?
o: All three have cells of the same length
questions.x: Skeletal muscle fibres are long multinucleate cells that may run much of the length of a muscle. Smooth muscle cells are short spindles, and cardiac cells are short and branched.

questions.q: Thick filaments are 1.6 µm and each thin filament 1.0 µm long. A sarcomere is stretched to 3.8 µm and then stimulated. It will:
o: Produce its greatest force, because the H zone is widest
Shorten normally, because calcium is still released
Produce no force, because thick and thin filaments no longer overlap
Produce force only by shortening its thick filaments
questions.x: Thin filaments reach 1.0 µm in from each Z line, but the thick filaments start (3.8 − 1.6) ÷ 2 = 1.1 µm in, so there is no overlap. Without overlap no cross-bridges can form, even though calcium is released.

questions.q: Inside the lacunae of cartilage, chondrocytes are usually seen:
o: In long rows of ten or more cells
Linked to each other by canaliculi
Singly or in small groups of two to four
Arranged in rings around a central canal
questions.x: Chondrocytes lie in lacunae either singly or in small groups of two to four. Canaliculi and rings around a central canal are features of bone, not cartilage.

questions.q: A relaxed sarcomere is 2.5 µm long. Each thin filament extends 1.0 µm from its Z line. How wide is the H zone?
questions.x: The H zone is the central gap between the tips of the thin filaments from the two Z lines: 2.5 − (1.0 + 1.0) = 0.5 µm. The value 1.5 µm comes from wrongly subtracting only one thin filament.

questions.q: When the calcium concentration in the sarcoplasm falls after stimulation stops, contraction ends because:
o: Calcium leaves troponin and tropomyosin covers the binding sites on actin again
Myosin heads lose their ATPase activity permanently
Actin filaments break away from the Z lines
questions.x: Without calcium bound, troponin lets tropomyosin slip back over the myosin-binding sites, so no new cross-bridges can form. The proteins are not damaged and the filaments stay attached to the Z lines.

questions.q: A drug stops the calcium pumps of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, while ATP supply stays normal. After one stimulus the muscle fibre will most directly:
o: Fail to contract at all, because no calcium is released
Lose its ability to make acetylcholine
Stay contracted, because calcium remains in the sarcoplasm
questions.x: Calcium is still released on stimulation, so the fibre contracts, but it cannot be pumped back. With calcium left on troponin, the binding sites stay exposed and relaxation fails.

questions.q: In severe hemophilia, repeated internal bleeding commonly occurs into the:
questions.x: Bleeding into joints (and muscles) is a typical feature of severe hemophilia and can damage the joints over time.

questions.q: In the cross AaBbCcDd × AaBbCcDd, with independent genes, what fraction of the offspring is homozygous dominant for all four genes?
questions.x: For each gene, P(homozygous dominant) = 1/4. For four genes: (1/4)⁴ = 1/256.

questions.q: The human Y chromosome decides maleness because it carries a gene that causes the embryo to develop:
questions.x: A gene on the Y (the testis-determining factor) makes the embryonic gonads develop into testes. Without it, ovaries form.

questions.q: Gene X is 12 map units from gene Y, and gene Y is 7 map units from gene Z. Ignoring double crossovers, the distance between X and Z could be:
questions.x: Z may lie on the far side of Y from X (12 + 7 = 19) or between X and Y (12 − 7 = 5). Without the X–Z value, both orders are possible.

questions.q: Two genes give an F2 ratio very close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. This shows that the two genes are:
o: Two alleles of the same gene
questions.x: A 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio is the result of independent assortment. Linked genes give an excess of parental types instead.

questions.q: A white-eyed female Drosophila is crossed with a white-eyed male. The offspring are expected to be:
o: All white-eyed, both males and females
questions.x: Both parents carry only the white allele (XʷXʷ and XʷY), so every offspring receives Xʷ and no red allele. All are white-eyed.

questions.q: A woman is heterozygous for an X-linked allele. What fraction of her sons are expected to receive this allele?
questions.x: Each son gets one of her two X chromosomes at random, so on average half receive the allele. Sons get nothing X-linked from the father.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of the human Y chromosome?
o: It is smaller than the X chromosome
It is passed from a father to his sons
It is present only in males
It carries the gene for red–green colour vision
questions.x: The colour-vision genes lie on the X chromosome, which is why colour blindness is X-linked. The other statements about the Y are true.

questions.q: During ventricular systole, the right and left ventricles contract:
o: One after the other, the right first and then the left
At the same time, sending blood into the pulmonary trunk and aorta together
One after the other, the left first and then the right
questions.x: Both ventricles contract together, so equal volumes of blood are sent into the pulmonary trunk and the aorta in each beat.

questions.q: If the pulmonary semilunar valve does not close properly, blood will leak back:
o: From the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle when the ventricles relax
From the right ventricle into the right atrium when the ventricles contract
From the aorta into the left ventricle when the ventricles relax
From the left atrium into the pulmonary veins when the atria contract
questions.x: The pulmonary semilunar valve lies between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk and should close when the ventricles relax. A leaky valve lets blood flow back into the right ventricle at that time.

questions.q: The adenoids are lymphoid tissue found at the:
o: Junction of the small and large intestines
Back of the nasal cavity, above the throat
questions.x: Adenoids (pharyngeal tonsils) sit at the back of the nose where it joins the throat, trapping pathogens that are breathed in.

questions.q: The thymus helps lymphocytes become mature T cells partly by secreting the hormone:
questions.x: The thymus releases thymosin, which promotes the maturation of T-lymphocytes. Thyroxine comes from the thyroid gland, a different organ.

questions.q: The inferior vena cava returns blood to the right atrium from the:
o: Lower parts of the body, such as the abdomen and legs
questions.x: The inferior vena cava collects blood from the parts of the body below the heart. The head and arms drain into the superior vena cava.

questions.q: A vaccine contains antigens, whereas an antiserum used for treatment contains:
questions.x: A vaccine stimulates the body to make its own antibodies (active immunity). An antiserum supplies ready-made antibodies (passive immunity).

questions.q: Each of the two arms of a Y-shaped antibody molecule is formed by:
o: One light chain and part of one heavy chain
One heavy chain and two light chains
questions.x: An antibody has two heavy and two light chains. Each arm consists of a whole light chain alongside the upper part of a heavy chain; the stem is formed by the two heavy chains alone.

questions.q: In a heavy smoker, 10% of the haemoglobin is present as carboxyhaemoglobin. By about how much is the maximum oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood reduced?
questions.x: Haemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide cannot carry oxygen, so if 10% is carboxyhaemoglobin, about 10% of the oxygen-carrying capacity is lost.

questions.q: Exhaled air contains more oxygen than the air in the alveoli. The reason is that exhaled air:
o: Is mixed with air from the airways (dead space) that took no part in gas exchange
Picks up oxygen released by the trachea
Contains oxygen made by red blood cells
Has passed through the nose, which adds oxygen
questions.x: The last part of each inspiration stays in the trachea and bronchi, where no exchange occurs. On expiration this fresher air mixes with alveolar air, so exhaled air has a higher oxygen level than alveolar air.

questions.q: Filter-tipped cigarettes are still harmful mainly because the filter:
o: Adds extra nicotine to the smoke
Removes all oxygen from the smoke
Makes the smoke enter the blood without passing through the lungs
Removes only part of the tar and does not remove carbon monoxide
questions.x: A filter traps some tar particles but lets through gases such as carbon monoxide and much of the tar and nicotine. Smokers of filtered cigarettes still have a high risk of lung disease.

questions.q: A gallstone blocks a person's common bile duct. Which of the following is expected?
o: Undigested starch in the faeces and low blood glucose
Failure of protein digestion in the stomach
Pale, fatty faeces and poor absorption of vitamin K
Darker faeces and increased absorption of fats
questions.x: Without bile, fats are poorly emulsified and absorbed, so they appear in the faeces, which are also pale because bile pigments are missing. Fat-soluble vitamins such as K are absorbed with fats, so their uptake falls.

questions.q: In the neck and chest, the oesophagus lies:
o: In front of the trachea, just under the skin
Inside the cartilage rings of the trachea
Beside the trachea but outside the thoracic cavity
Behind the trachea and in front of the vertebral column
questions.x: The oesophagus runs down behind (dorsal to) the trachea and in front of the backbone, through the thorax, and then pierces the diaphragm. The tracheal rings are open at the back, where the oesophagus lies.

questions.q: The 'wisdom teeth', usually the last teeth to appear, in the late teens or later, are the:
questions.x: Wisdom teeth are the third (last) molars at the back of each half jaw. They erupt last, usually from the late teens onwards, and sometimes not at all.

questions.q: People with chronic kidney failure often develop weak bones. One reason is that healthy kidneys normally:
o: Convert vitamin D into its active form, which helps absorb calcium
questions.x: Active vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium from the gut. Damaged kidneys make less of it, so bones lose calcium. Parathyroid hormone comes from the parathyroid glands.

questions.q: Urinary tract infections are more common in women than in men mainly because:
o: The female bladder has no sphincter
The female urethra is much shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder more easily
questions.x: Bacteria usually enter from outside through the urethra. A short urethra gives them a shorter route to the bladder, so infection is more common in women.

questions.q: Tubular secretion usually needs energy because it:
o: Forces fluid out under blood pressure
Moves substances into the tubule against their concentration gradient
questions.x: Secretion concentrates substances such as H+ in the tubule fluid, often against a gradient, so tubule cells use active transport. Filtration, by contrast, is powered by blood pressure.

questions.q: Blood in the efferent arteriole leaving a glomerulus is:
o: Still oxygenated, since the glomerulus filters rather than supplying oxygen to tissues
Deoxygenated, having supplied oxygen to Bowman's capsule
Venous blood on its way to the renal vein
questions.x: The glomerulus is a filter, not a site of tissue supply, so blood leaves it still oxygenated in an arteriole. It gives up its oxygen later, in the peritubular capillaries.

questions.q: A healthy adult can safely donate one kidney to a relative because:
o: The donated kidney grows back within months
The liver takes over the work of the kidney
Each kidney works for only half the day
One healthy kidney can do enough work to keep the body healthy
questions.x: The kidneys have a large spare capacity, so one healthy kidney is enough for normal life. A removed kidney does not regrow.

questions.q: Keeping the osmotic concentration of the blood constant is important mainly because:
o: Enzymes in the blood need extra salt to work
Otherwise the heart would stop pumping
Body cells would otherwise gain or lose water by osmosis and swell or shrink
Otherwise urea would turn back into ammonia
questions.x: If blood became too dilute, cells such as red cells would take in water and could burst; if too concentrated, they would lose water and shrink. Osmoregulation prevents both.

questions.q: Nearly all of the 180 litres of filtrate formed each day returns to the circulation through the:
o: Peritubular capillaries, including the vasa recta
questions.x: Reabsorbed fluid enters the low-pressure peritubular capillaries and vasa recta, which drain into the renal vein. The glomerular capillaries only lose fluid.

questions.q: A diuretic is a substance that:
o: Increases the volume of urine produced
Decreases the volume of urine produced
questions.x: 'Diuresis' means a large output of urine, so a diuretic increases urine volume. Alcohol and caffeine have this effect; ADH, an antidiuretic, does the opposite.

questions.q: A cook works long hours in a hot kitchen, drinks little water and passes small amounts of dark urine. Which advice lowers his risk of kidney stones?
o: Drink enough water to pass plenty of pale urine
Drink as little as possible to rest the kidneys
questions.x: Plenty of water keeps urine dilute so salts stay dissolved. Extra meat, salt and vitamin D all raise stone risk.

questions.q: Edward Jenner made the first vaccine against smallpox by using material from:
questions.x: In 1796 Jenner inoculated a boy with material from cowpox sores; the mild cowpox virus protected him against the related smallpox virus. Smallpox is caused by a virus, not a bacterium.

questions.q: Gene therapy is most suitable for treating disorders that are:
o: Due to injuries such as fractures
Caused by a defect in a single gene
questions.x: Gene therapy adds a working copy of a gene, so it suits disorders such as cystic fibrosis or SCID that are caused by one faulty gene. Infections, injuries and diet-related problems are not gene defects.

questions.q: A plasmid carries genes for resistance to ampicillin and tetracycline. A foreign gene is inserted into the middle of the tetracycline-resistance gene. Bacteria carrying this recombinant plasmid will:
o: Grow on tetracycline but not on ampicillin
Grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline
questions.x: Inserting the gene into the tetracycline-resistance gene disrupts it (insertional inactivation), so those bacteria become sensitive to tetracycline. The ampicillin-resistance gene is untouched, so they still grow on ampicillin.

questions.q: In industry, a cheap reactant such as air or water is often used in excess. The main reason is to:
o: Make the cheap reactant the limiting reactant
Make sure the more expensive reactant becomes limiting and is fully used
Change the mole ratio in the balanced equation
questions.x: Using excess of the cheap reactant makes the costly one limiting, so none of it is wasted. The mole ratio of the equation never changes, and the theoretical yield cannot exceed 100%.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
questions.x: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 g mol⁻¹. Mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g.

questions.q: In the contact process, 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃. The mole ratio of O₂ to SO₃ is:
questions.x: The coefficients are 1 for O₂ and 2 for SO₃, so the ratio O₂ : SO₃ is 1 : 2. The ratio 2 : 1 is the inverted fraction.

questions.q: Which quantum number describes the orientation of an orbital in space?
questions.x: m gives the orientation of an orbital, e.g. px, py, pz. n gives the shell and size, l the shape, and s the spin of the electron.

questions.q: Which subshell is filled immediately before 4f?
questions.x: The order is …5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p. 6s has n + l = 6 and 4f has n + l = 7, so 6s fills just before 4f.

questions.q: Using R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, one dm³ atm is equal to about:
questions.x: 8.314/0.0821 ≈ 101.3, so 1 dm³ atm ≈ 101.3 J. Dividing the other way round gives the wrong 0.0099 J.

questions.q: The pressure on a fixed amount of an ideal gas is halved while its absolute temperature is doubled. Its volume becomes:
questions.x: V = nRT/P. Doubling T doubles V and halving P doubles it again, so the volume becomes four times larger.

questions.q: The volume of a fixed mass of gas is halved at constant temperature. The number of collisions per second on each unit area of the wall:
o: Stays the same, so the pressure stays the same
Doubles, but the pressure stays the same
questions.x: The same molecules at the same speed in half the volume are twice as crowded, so they strike each area of wall twice as often. This doubles the pressure, as Boyle's law predicts.

questions.q: The ideal gas equation PV = nRT becomes Boyle's law when:
o: n and P are kept constant
n and T are kept constant
P and T are kept constant
n and V are kept constant
questions.x: With n and T fixed, nRT is a constant, so PV = constant, which is Boyle's law. Constant n and P gives Charles's law instead.

questions.q: A liquid expands on heating because its molecules:
o: Move faster and push one another slightly farther apart
questions.x: Heating raises the kinetic energy of the molecules, so they move more vigorously and their average separation increases. The molecules themselves do not grow.

questions.q: Whether an ionic solid dissolves in water depends mainly on the balance between:
o: Its melting point and the boiling point of water
Its lattice energy and the hydration energies of its ions
Its density and the density of water
Its ionisation energy and its electron affinity
questions.x: Energy is needed to break the lattice and is released when ions are hydrated; if hydration energy is comparable to or larger than lattice energy, the solid dissolves.

questions.q: Of the six parameters that describe a unit cell, how many are angles?
questions.x: The six parameters are three edge lengths (a, b, c) and three angles (α, β, γ).

questions.q: A little HCl is added to a solution of ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH). The degree of ionisation of the ethanoic acid:
o: Increases, because HCl supplies more H⁺
Decreases, because of the common H⁺ ion
Stays the same, because HCl is a strong acid
Increases, because CH₃COO⁻ ions are removed
questions.x: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺. Extra H⁺ from HCl shifts this to the left, so less ethanoic acid ionises.

questions.q: On a graph of concentration against time for a reversible reaction in a closed vessel, equilibrium is reached when:
o: The curves for reactants and products become flat (horizontal)
The curves for reactants and products cross each other
All the curves fall to zero
The product curve rises above the reactant curve
questions.x: At equilibrium, concentrations stop changing, so their curves level off. They need not be equal, so crossing does not mark equilibrium.

questions.q: A buffer can also be made from two salts of a polyprotic acid. Which mixture is such a buffer?
questions.x: H₂PO₄⁻ acts as a weak acid and HPO₄²⁻ as its conjugate base, so the pair resists pH change. The other pairs are neutral salts of strong acids and bases.

questions.q: A reaction is second order in X and first order in Y, and k = 5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹. Calculate its speed at [X] = 0.2 and [Y] = 0.1 mol dm⁻³.
questions.x: Rate = 5 × (0.2)² × 0.1 = 5 × 0.04 × 0.1 = 0.02 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Forgetting to square [X] gives 0.1.

questions.q: For 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂, oxygen is formed at 0.02 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. At what rate is H₂O₂ used up?
questions.x: 2 mol H₂O₂ are used for every 1 mol O₂ formed, so H₂O₂ is used twice as fast: 2 × 0.02 = 0.04 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

questions.q: Which statement about the internal energy, E, of a system is correct?
o: It can be measured directly with a thermometer
It depends on how the system reached its present state
Its absolute value cannot be measured; only the change, ΔE, can be found
It is zero for every element at room temperature
questions.x: Internal energy includes all kinetic and potential energies of the particles, so its total cannot be measured. ΔE can be found, and E is a state function.

questions.q: The SI unit of energy, used for internal energy, heat and work, is named after:
questions.x: The joule (J) is named after J. P. Joule, who studied the relation between heat and work. Watt, newton and pascal are units of power, force and pressure.

questions.q: Which process does NOT take place spontaneously?
o: A gas spreading out to fill an empty container
Ice melting in a warm room
Heat flowing by itself from a cold body to a hot body
questions.x: Heat flows naturally from hot to cold; the reverse needs outside work, as in a refrigerator. The other changes happen on their own.

questions.q: The electrochemical series arranges elements in order of their:
questions.x: The electrochemical series lists electrodes in order of their standard electrode potential values.

questions.q: In H₂O₂ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O, hydrogen peroxide acts as:
o: An oxidising agent, as its oxygen falls from −1 to −2
A reducing agent, as its oxygen rises from −1 to 0
An acid only, with no change in oxidation number
A reducing agent, as its hydrogen falls from +1 to 0
questions.x: Iodide is oxidised to iodine, so H₂O₂ is reduced: oxygen goes from −1 in H₂O₂ to −2 in water.

questions.q: In ethyne, HC≡CH, how many unhybridised p orbitals does each carbon atom have?
questions.x: Each carbon is sp hybridised, using one s and one p orbital. The other two p orbitals stay unhybridised and form the two π bonds of the triple bond.

questions.q: Which isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene has zero dipole moment?
o: The cis isomer, because the two Cl atoms are on the same side
The trans isomer, because the two C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions
Both isomers, because they have the same atoms
Neither isomer, because C–Cl bonds are always polar
questions.x: In the trans isomer the two C–Cl bond dipoles are opposite and cancel. In the cis isomer they point to the same side, giving a net dipole moment.

questions.q: Breaking all the bonds in one mole of water vapour, H₂O(g) → 2H(g) + O(g), needs 926 kJ. The average O–H bond energy is:
questions.x: Each water molecule has two O–H bonds, so the average O–H bond energy = 926 ÷ 2 = 463 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: Calcium reacts steadily with cold water, while magnesium reacts only very slowly with it. This is mainly because calcium:
o: Has a smaller atom and higher ionisation energies
Forms a more insoluble hydroxide that protects it
Has a larger atom and lower ionisation energies, so it loses its outer electrons more easily
Has more valence electrons than magnesium
questions.x: Reactivity of Group II metals increases down the group as atoms get larger and the two outer electrons are lost more easily.

questions.q: When an alkaline earth metal M burns in chlorine gas, the salt produced has the formula:
questions.x: Group II metals form M²⁺ ions, so two Cl⁻ ions are needed for each metal ion: M + Cl₂ → MCl₂.

questions.q: Which compound is classed as organic even though it contains no hydrogen?
questions.x: CCl₄ is a derivative of methane in which every H is replaced by Cl, so it is organic. CO, carbonates and carbides are studied as inorganic carbon compounds.

questions.q: Maleic acid and fumaric acid both have the structure HOOCCH=CHCOOH but different properties. They are:
questions.x: They differ only in the arrangement of the –COOH groups about the C=C bond: maleic acid is cis and fumaric acid is trans.

questions.q: In an addition reaction, two reactant molecules:
o: Exchange atoms to form two products
Each split into two smaller molecules
Combine to form a single product
Lose a small molecule such as water
questions.x: In addition, atoms add across a multiple bond and one product results, e.g. C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Losing a small molecule describes elimination.

questions.q: The reaction HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃ (over heated nickel) is an example of:
questions.x: Hydrogen atoms add across the triple bond and no atom is replaced, so the reaction is addition (hydrogenation).

questions.q: How many Kekulé structures are used to show resonance in benzene?
questions.x: Benzene is shown as a resonance hybrid of two Kekulé structures, which differ only in where the three double bonds are placed.

questions.q: How many electrons are present in the outer shell of a chlorine free radical, Cl•?
questions.x: A chlorine atom has 7 outer electrons, one of them unpaired. Gaining an eighth electron would make it the chloride ion, Cl⁻, which is not a radical.

questions.q: 15.6 g of benzene is brominated with Br₂/FeBr₃ to give bromobenzene, C₆H₅Br. What mass of bromobenzene is formed if the yield is 100%? (C 12, H 1, Br 80)
questions.x: Moles of benzene = 15.6/78 = 0.2. M(C₆H₅Br) = 72 + 5 + 80 = 157, so mass = 0.2 × 157 = 31.4 g. 32.0 g is the mass of Br₂ used.

questions.q: Which reaction takes place with benzene but NOT with hexane?
o: Complete combustion in air to give CO₂ and H₂O
Reaction with chlorine in ultraviolet light
Nitration with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄ at 50–55 °C
questions.x: Benzene's π electrons attract the NO₂⁺ electrophile, so it is nitrated under mild conditions; hexane has no π electrons and is not. Both burn and both react with Cl₂ in UV light, and neither decolourises cold KMnO₄.

questions.q: Ethane is chlorinated further, giving products with molecular formula C₂H₃Cl₃. Counting different positional arrangements of chlorine, these products exist as how many isomers?
questions.x: The three chlorines can all be on one carbon (1,1,1-trichloroethane) or two on one carbon and one on the other (1,1,2-trichloroethane). No other arrangement is possible.

questions.q: Which statement about the physical properties of alkyl halides is correct?
o: They form strong hydrogen bonds with water
Their boiling points fall as the halogen becomes heavier
They boil lower than alkanes with the same number of carbons
Bromoalkanes and iodoalkanes are generally denser than water
questions.x: Heavy bromine and iodine atoms make these compounds denser than water. Alkyl halides cannot hydrogen-bond with water, their boiling points rise with a heavier halogen, and they boil higher than the parent alkanes.

questions.q: 0.4 mol of ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH₂CH₂OH, reacts completely with excess sodium. What volume of hydrogen forms at STP? (1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Each molecule has two –OH groups, and 2 –OH give 1 H₂, so 1 mol diol gives 1 mol H₂. 0.4 mol H₂ × 22.4 = 8.96 dm³. 4.48 dm³ counts only one –OH group.

questions.q: Which pair of compounds reacts in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to give ethyl methanoate, HCOOC₂H₅?
questions.x: In an ester name, the alkyl group ('ethyl') comes from the alcohol and the '-oate' part from the acid ('methanoate'), so the reactants are methanoic acid and ethanol. Ethanoic acid with methanol gives the isomer methyl ethanoate.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of the dihydric phenol C₆H₄(OH)₂ with the two –OH groups on neighbouring carbon atoms (catechol) is:
questions.x: Neighbouring (ortho) positions are 1 and 2, so catechol is benzene-1,2-diol. Benzene-1,3-diol is resorcinol and benzene-1,4-diol is quinol (hydroquinone).

questions.q: Vapour of propan-2-ol is passed over heated copper at about 300 °C. The organic product is:
questions.x: Hot copper removes hydrogen (dehydrogenation): (CH₃)₂CHOH → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone; propanal would come from propan-1-ol.

questions.q: The Cannizzaro reaction, in which an aldehyde is warmed with concentrated NaOH to give an alcohol and a carboxylate salt, is shown by aldehydes that:
o: Have at least two α-hydrogen atoms
Are ketones with a methyl group
questions.x: Aldehydes without α-hydrogen, such as methanal and benzaldehyde, cannot form a carbanion and so cannot do aldol condensation; instead one molecule is oxidised and another reduced (Cannizzaro).

questions.q: Which carboxylic acid and alcohol react together to form the ester CH₃CH₂COOCH₃?
questions.x: The acyl part CH₃CH₂CO– comes from propanoic acid and –OCH₃ from methanol. Ethanoic acid with ethanol gives an isomer, ethyl ethanoate.

questions.q: Some enzymes work only when a metal ion such as Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺ is present. Such an inorganic ion is called an enzyme:
questions.x: Inorganic ions that an enzyme needs for activity are activators (inorganic cofactors). A coenzyme is an organic molecule, often made from a vitamin.

questions.q: Compared with joining parts by rivets or bolts, an advantage of using an adhesive is that it:
o: Always gives a joint stronger than the materials themselves
Can always be taken apart easily without damage
Works at any temperature without softening
Spreads the load over the whole bonded area and can join unlike materials
questions.x: An adhesive needs no holes, spreads stress evenly and can bond different materials such as metal to plastic. Adhesive joints are not always stronger than the materials and many soften when hot.

questions.q: Power delivered by a force can be written as the scalar product of:
questions.x: P = F · v, a scalar product. Force · displacement gives work, not power.

questions.q: A car's velocity is negative and its acceleration is also negative. The car is:
o: Slowing down in the negative direction
Speeding up in the positive direction
Speeding up in the negative direction
questions.x: When velocity and acceleration have the same sign they point the same way, so the speed increases. Here both point in the negative direction.

questions.q: A 50 kg astronaut at rest in space throws a 5 kg toolbox away at 2 m s⁻¹. The astronaut moves off at:
o: 2 m s⁻¹ opposite to the toolbox
0.2 m s⁻¹ opposite to the toolbox
20 m s⁻¹ opposite to the toolbox
0.2 m s⁻¹ in the same direction as the toolbox
questions.x: Total momentum stays zero: 50v = 5 × 2, so v = 0.2 m s⁻¹, in the direction opposite to the toolbox.

questions.q: Ignoring air resistance, the path of a stone thrown horizontally from the top of a cliff is:
questions.x: Horizontal distance grows as t and vertical drop as t², so y is proportional to x²: half of a parabola starting at its highest point.

questions.q: A horizontal force of 12 N acts on a 4 kg block on a smooth horizontal surface. The acceleration of the block is:
questions.x: By Newton's second law a = F/m = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m s⁻². 48 m s⁻² multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.q: A 1 kg ball and a 3 kg ball are launched with the same velocity. Ignoring air resistance, their paths are:
o: Different, the heavier ball going less far
Different, the heavier ball going higher
Exactly the same, with equal ranges and maximum heights
Different, the lighter ball landing first
questions.x: Without air resistance both have acceleration g and the same initial velocity, so the motion does not depend on mass and the paths are identical.

questions.q: At the highest point of an oblique projectile's path, which component of its velocity is zero?
questions.x: At the top the projectile stops rising and is about to fall, so the vertical component is zero. The horizontal component is unchanged.

questions.q: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m s⁻¹ is braked to rest on a level road. Ignoring other losses, the heat produced in the brakes is:
questions.x: Heat = KE lost = ½ × 1000 × 20² = 2 × 10⁵ J. Forgetting the ½ gives 4 × 10⁵ J; forgetting to square gives 1 × 10⁴ J.

questions.q: A 2 kg box is lifted vertically through 5 m and then carried 10 m horizontally at that height. The total gain in its gravitational potential energy is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: Only the vertical rise changes gravitational PE: 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. The horizontal movement is perpendicular to gravity, so it adds nothing.

questions.q: If both the mass of a body and its height above the ground are doubled, its gravitational potential energy becomes:
questions.x: PE = mgh is proportional to both m and h, so doubling each gives 2 × 2 = 4 times.

questions.q: A point moves through an arc of length s on a circle of radius r. Its angular displacement θ in radians is given by:
questions.x: Angle in radians is arc length divided by radius, θ = s/r. Multiplying s by r or including 2π are common slips.

questions.q: For a compressible gas in steady flow through a pipe, the quantity that stays the same at every cross-section is:
questions.x: Conservation of mass requires the mass flow rate ρAv to be the same everywhere. Av is constant only when the density does not change.

questions.q: A thin thread of ink is fed into water flowing slowly through a glass tube; it stays as a straight line. When the water speed is increased a lot, the ink spreads out across the whole tube. This shows that:
o: At high speed the water becomes non-viscous
The ink becomes more viscous at high speed
Continuity no longer applies at high speed
At high speed the flow changes from laminar to turbulent
questions.x: A straight ink thread marks laminar flow; mixing across the tube shows eddies, i.e. turbulence, which sets in above a critical speed.

questions.q: Liquids such as water are usually treated as incompressible because:
o: Their density hardly changes even under a large pressure
They always flow in a laminar way
questions.x: Incompressible means the density stays constant. Liquids change volume very little under pressure, so this is a good approximation; it says nothing about viscosity or the type of flow.

questions.q: An ideal fluid flows through a pipe. Where the cross-sectional area of the pipe is doubled, the speed of the fluid:
questions.x: By continuity Av = constant, so doubling A halves v.

questions.q: Consider the particles of a string vibrating as a standing (stationary) wave. Which of these is true?
o: All particles that are not at nodes reach their maximum displacement at the same instant
Each particle reaches its maximum displacement slightly after its neighbour
The particles at the nodes vibrate with the largest amplitude
The wave pattern moves along the string at speed fλ
questions.x: Particles within a loop are in phase and adjacent loops are in antiphase, so the whole string reaches its extreme shape at one instant. A gradual phase lag along the medium belongs to a progressive wave.

questions.q: The second harmonic of a stretched string is 240 Hz. The frequency of its fourth harmonic is:
questions.x: The fundamental is 240/2 = 120 Hz, so the fourth harmonic is 4 × 120 = 480 Hz.

questions.q: Two coherent sources oscillate exactly out of step with each other (antiphase) and send out waves of equal amplitude. At a point that is one wavelength farther from one source than from the other, the waves:
o: Give an amplitude equal to that of one wave
Give a maximum only if the sources are far apart
questions.x: A path difference of λ adds a phase difference of 2π, which changes nothing, so the waves arrive with the sources' own phase difference of π. Equal amplitudes in opposite phase cancel.

questions.q: A lightning flash is seen and the thunder is heard 3 s later. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m s⁻¹ and treating the light as arriving instantly, the distance to the lightning is about:
questions.x: Light, an electromagnetic wave, is so fast that its travel time is negligible. Distance = 340 × 3 = 1020 m.

questions.q: Two waves overlap at a point. One gives a displacement of +5 mm there, and the resultant displacement is +1 mm. The displacement due to the other wave is:
questions.x: Resultant = sum of displacements, so the other wave gives 1 − 5 = −4 mm.

questions.q: A wave travels at 12 m s⁻¹ and has a wavelength of 3 m. The time period of the wave is:
questions.x: f = v/λ = 12/3 = 4 Hz, so T = 1/f = 0.25 s. Stopping at 4 gives the frequency, not the period.

questions.q: In deriving Cp − Cv = R, the first law is applied to n moles heated through ΔT at constant pressure. The heat supplied, nCpΔT, is set equal to:
questions.x: At constant pressure the heat raises the internal energy (nCvΔT) and does work PΔV. With PΔV = nRΔT this gives Cp = Cv + R.

questions.q: For an ideal gas of molar mass M, the difference between the specific heats per kilogram, cp − cv, is equal to:
questions.x: Per mole, Cp − Cv = R. Dividing by the molar mass M (kg per mole) changes per-mole values into per-kilogram values, so cp − cv = R/M.

questions.q: A charged dust particle of mass 1 × 10⁻⁶ kg stays at rest in a uniform electric field of 2 × 10³ N C⁻¹ that points vertically upward. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², the charge on the particle is:
questions.x: The electric force must balance the weight, so it acts upward along the field, meaning the charge is positive. q = mg/E = 1 × 10⁻⁵ / 2 × 10³ = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C.

questions.q: The electric field around a charge is a field of force, just as the gravitational field around the Earth is. In the gravitational field, the quantity that plays the role of charge is:
questions.x: Electric field strength is force per unit charge; gravitational field strength is force per unit mass (N kg⁻¹). Weight is the force itself, not the property that experiences it.

questions.q: Find the repulsion between two identical 3 μC charges held 30 cm from each other. (k = 9 × 10⁹ SI units)
questions.x: F = kq²/r² = 9 × 10⁹ × (3 × 10⁻⁶)² / (0.3)² = 0.081 / 0.09 = 0.9 N. Forgetting to square r gives 0.27 N.

questions.q: An uncharged capacitor is connected in series with a 4 kΩ resistor to a 12 V battery. The current just after the switch is closed is:
questions.x: At the first instant the capacitor has no charge, so no voltage across it; the full 12 V is across the resistor: I = 12 / 4000 = 3 mA.

questions.q: A filament lamp and a diode are non-ohmic devices. Plotted as current against voltage, their characteristic graphs are:
o: Curves, not straight lines through the origin
questions.x: Ohmic devices give a straight line through the origin because V/I is constant. For non-ohmic devices, such as a diode or filament lamp, V/I changes, so the graph curves.

questions.q: A coil lies in a uniform field with its normal along the field, so the flux is BA. It is turned through 180°. The flux through it is now:
questions.x: After a half turn the normal points opposite to B, so θ = 180° and Φ = BA cos 180° = −BA.

questions.q: The magnetic force on a moving charge can change the particle's:
o: Direction of motion but not its speed
questions.x: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it only bends the path. It does no work, so the speed stays the same.

questions.q: A metal loop is pulled out of a region of uniform magnetic field. The force on the induced current in the loop:
o: Helps the pull, drawing the loop out faster
Acts at right angles to the pull and does no work
Opposes the pull, tending to keep the loop in the field
Is zero because the field is uniform
questions.x: Pulling the loop out reduces the flux. The induced current opposes this change, so the force on it acts against the pull.

questions.q: Warm bodies emit a radiation that is used in TV remote controls and thermal imaging cameras. This radiation is:
questions.x: Infrared is emitted by warm objects and is used in remote controls and thermal imaging. Ultraviolet comes mainly from very hot sources such as the Sun.

questions.q: An advantage of a bridge rectifier over the two-diode full-wave rectifier is that the bridge circuit:
o: Does not need a centre-tapped transformer
Produces pure DC without any filter
questions.x: The bridge uses four diodes but works with an ordinary transformer secondary, whereas the two-diode circuit needs a centre tap. Its output is still pulsating DC without a filter.

questions.q: Photons of energy 4.5 eV fall on a metal with work function 2.5 eV. The stopping potential needed to halt the fastest photoelectrons is:
questions.x: KEmax = 4.5 − 2.5 = 2 eV, and eV₀ = KEmax, so the stopping potential is 2 V.

questions.q: The ground-state energy of hydrogen is −13.6 eV and the level energies vary as 1/n². What is the energy of the electron in the fourth orbit (n = 4)?
questions.x: E₄ = −13.6/4² = −13.6/16 = −0.85 eV. Dividing by 4 instead of 16 gives −3.4 eV, which is really the n = 2 level.

questions.q: Which nuclear radiation produces the most ionisation per centimetre of its path in air?
questions.x: Alpha particles are heavy and doubly charged, so they ionise very strongly and lose their energy within a few centimetres of air.

questions.q: On the morning of her chemistry practical, Fatima woke early and revised her notes on titration. After breakfast she checked that her lab coat and calculator were in her bag. On the way to college she realised she had left her roll-number slip at home, so she phoned her brother, who brought it on his motorbike. She reached the laboratory ten minutes before the start. Why did Fatima phone her brother?
o: She was late and needed a lift
She had left her roll-number slip at home
She had left her lab coat at home
questions.x: The passage says she phoned her brother because she had left her roll-number slip at home. She had already checked that her lab coat and calculator were in her bag, and she arrived early.

questions.q: Years later, Sara still had a vivid memory of her first day at medical college: the smell of the new white coat, the long echoing corridors, the nervous laughter of the girls beside her, and the exact words of the professor's welcome. As used in the passage, 'vivid' means:
questions.x: Sara remembers smells, sounds and exact words, so her memory is clear and detailed. 'Faint and unclear' is the opposite.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "The doctor told the patient not ___ heavy weights for a month."
questions.x: 'Tell someone not to do something' uses 'not' before the to-infinitive.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "Rarely ___ such heavy snow in Lahore."
questions.x: After a negative adverb such as 'Rarely' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: 'do we see'.

questions.q: Change into the passive voice: "People speak Urdu all over Pakistan."
o: Urdu was spoken all over Pakistan.
Urdu is speaking all over Pakistan.
Urdu is spoken all over Pakistan.
Urdu has spoken all over Pakistan.
questions.x: The simple present passive is 'is' + past participle; a vague agent like 'people' is usually left out.

questions.q: Choose the correct pair: "The flight is due to land ___ 5:30 ___ the morning."
questions.x: 'At' is used with clock times and 'in' with parts of the day such as 'the morning'.

questions.q: "Ali's handwriting is so illegible that even he cannot read his own chemistry notes a week later." The word 'illegible' means:
questions.x: 'Illegible' means not clear enough to be read; even the writer cannot read it.

questions.q: Which pair shows two words of similar meaning in which the second is clearly STRONGER in feeling than the first?
questions.x: 'Loathe' means to hate intensely, a stronger feeling than 'dislike'; in the reversed pair the second word is weaker, and 'begin – commence' differ only in formality.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: "Mathematics ____ my favourite subject this year."
questions.x: Names of subjects ending in -s, such as mathematics, physics and economics, are singular and take a singular verb.

questions.q: A city's transport department says: "Our new buses will run every 10 minutes so that people leave their cars at home." Which assumption does the department make?
o: Nobody in the city owns a car
Buses are faster than cars on every road
Some car users would switch to a frequent bus service
All buses in the city are new
questions.x: The plan only works if a frequent service would attract at least some car users. It does not need to assume buses beat cars on every road.

questions.q: Statement: Should smoking be banned inside hospitals? Argument I: Yes, smoke harms patients who are already ill. Argument II: No, smokers like to smoke wherever they want. Which argument is strong?
o: Both arguments I and II are strong
Neither argument I nor II is strong
questions.x: Argument I gives a real, important reason linked to patients' health. Argument II rests only on smokers' wishes, which is not a strong reason.

questions.q: Find the next number: 1, 4, 13, 40, ?
questions.x: Each term is 3 times the one before plus 1: 40 x 3 + 1 = 121.

questions.q: Find the next number: 5, 15, 8, 18, 11, 21, ?
questions.x: The steps alternate +10 and -7: 5, 15, 8, 18, 11, 21. The next step is -7: 21 - 7 = 14.

questions.q: Every W is an X, and at least one W is a Y. Which statement must be true?
o: At least one X is a Y
questions.x: The W that is a Y is also an X, because every W is an X; so at least one X is a Y. Nothing is said about Y that are not W, or about X that are not W.

questions.q: Exactly one of Ali, Bilal and Hamza broke a window. Ali says, "Bilal did it." Bilal says, "I did not do it." Hamza says, "I did not do it." If exactly one of the three is telling the truth, who broke the window?
questions.x: If Ali or Bilal did it, two of the statements would be true. Only if Hamza did it is just one statement (Bilal's) true.

questions.q: Statement: A few cases of cholera were reported in one village after floods. Courses of action: I. Health teams should be sent to the village to treat patients and test the drinking water. II. The whole province should be declared a disaster zone. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Health teams address the cases and their likely source. A few cases in one village do not justify declaring a whole province a disaster zone.

questions.q: Statement: Passengers at a city airport often miss their flights because of long queues at its single security counter. Courses of action: I. Security checks at the airport should be stopped. II. More security counters should be opened at busy times. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The queue comes from having one counter, so opening more counters fixes it. Removing security checks would put passengers in danger.

questions.q: Statement I: The college canteen ran out of food by noon. Statement II: The canteen's supplier did not deliver that morning. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: Without the morning delivery, the canteen had too little food for the day. The missed delivery caused the shortage.
